body: Architecture has always been shaped around people, and especially around the way they move. The coaching inn, the railway station, the bus depot, the airport and the highway service area were each built around a pause in a journey, and each was sized to the time that pause allowed. That pause is now changing. Fuel is getting more expensive, vehicles are learning to drive themselves, and road transport is turning to electricity. A car that once stopped for five minutes to fill its tank now stops for close to an hour to charge. Yet the places built for charging have hardly changed from the car parks and forecourts they replaced, and many drivers avoid them altogether by charging at home.

This thesis, the Powerhouse, proposes a sustainable charging cluster: an Electric Vehicle Powerhouse complex that will turn charging activities into an opportunity for enhanced civic / community engagements. The charge brings people to the site and keeps them there for a while. What the site offers in return depends on where it is. In a city it might be a gym or a place to work; on a busy freight corridor, a hostel with showers; in a town that lacks one, a market or a clinic. The Powerhouse is not one building repeated along the highway. It is a type that changes shape with the community around it.

Nor is it only for electric vehicles. The Powerhouse is open to everyone, including people who arrive on foot, by bus or by bicycle. Charging is the first case the thesis studies, but the idea reaches further. Almost any parking lot or leftover space at the edge of a road could become a Powerhouse, given a programme that serves its area.

Thousands of new charging sites will be built over the coming decades, and most are being planned as infrastructure and nothing more. This thesis asks how they could instead be woven into the everyday needs of the communities they sit in, and what it would take for those places to sustain themselves. It starts from a simple belief: that the energy transition is a chance to leave behind a better and greener landscape than the one we have now.

Transport uses a great deal of energy and wastes most of it. Of every hundred tonnes of greenhouse gas the United States emits, twenty-eight come from moving people and goods, more than from any other sector.<sup>1</sup> Across the world, road vehicles added just over six billion tonnes of carbon dioxide to the air in 2024.<sup>2</sup> Much of the problem is the engine. Fill a petrol car and roughly seven-tenths of that energy leaves through the exhaust and the radiator as heat; only about three-tenths actually moves the car. An electric car turns the ratio around, putting close to nine-tenths of what is in its battery to work.<sup>3</sup> At the wheels, it makes the same journey on roughly a third of the energy. Even so, an electric car is only as clean as the grid behind it. Economists who priced the damage done by driving electric across the United States found a clear benefit in California and a net harm in coal-heavy North Dakota.<sup>4</sup> This is one reason the Powerhouse generates its own energy.

The shift is happening fast. Five years ago electric cars were a niche of a few million sales a year. In 2025 buyers took home more than twenty million.<sup>5</sup> Automation is arriving alongside it. In ten American cities, Waymo now sells around half a million rides a week in cars with nobody at the wheel,<sup>6</sup> and since 2025 Aurora’s trucks have hauled paying freight between Dallas and Houston with the cab empty.<sup>7</sup> Cars have gone first. Freight and long-distance road transport are next. Speed is not the same as certainty, though. A review of ninety-four studies on electric-car adoption found that what actually persuades people to switch, public charging included, is far less settled than is usually assumed.<sup>8</sup>

For now, most charging happens at home. By the Department of Energy’s estimate, four of every five charges happen in a driveway or a garage.<sup>9</sup> That convenience has a cost. An electric car driven a typical American distance uses roughly three to four thousand kilowatt-hours of electricity a year, about a third of what an average home already uses.<sup>10</sup> Home charging moves the cost of the transition onto household bills, and is not an option for people who live in apartments or park on the street. Public charging will have to carry more of the load, and the places built for it will matter.

Stephen P. Holland, Erin T. Mansur, Nicholas Z. Muller, and Andrew J. Yates, “Are There Environmental Benefits from Driving Electric Vehicles? The Importance of Local Factors,” American Economic Review 106, no. 12 (2016): 3700.

body: Every kind of travel has produced its own architecture of waiting. The great railway stations of the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries were among the grandest buildings in their cities. Passengers arrived early and waited in vast halls, concourses and plazas, surrounded by restaurants, shops and newsstands. In New York, McKim, Mead and White borrowed the vaults of an ancient Roman bath for the waiting room of Pennsylvania Station, and Grand Central grew a small town of shops and restaurants around its concourse.<sup>11</sup> Airports went further, asking passengers to arrive up to two hours early and filling that time with lounges, shops and restaurants.

The roadside stop went the other way. For most of the twentieth century it meant the gas station, which settled early into a formula that hardly changed afterwards: a roof over the pumps, islands to pull up beside, and a booth where you paid on the way out.<sup>12</sup> It was built for grab-and-go, and it did that well. Five minutes is long enough to pay and too short for anything else.

The charging stop has inherited this form without its reason. The usual response is to add a few chargers to an existing car park. Public programmes such as the US National Electric Vehicle Infrastructure programme set standards for power and equipment, but say nothing about the place around the charger.<sup>13</sup> Drivers end up sitting in their cars beside a row of posts. Freight is worse off. American truckers already compete for somewhere to stop. Truck parking now ranks as the industry’s second most pressing problem after the economy, and drivers near the end of their legal hours often keep driving in search of a space.<sup>14</sup> Very few charging sites are built for heavy vehicles. A recent review of the American trucking market names charging infrastructure, alongside range and upfront cost, as one of the main obstacles to electric freight.<sup>15</sup> As trucks electrify, their stops will get longer, with nowhere designed to hold them. Marc Augé’s word for such spaces, non-places, fits them well: they are used all the time and belong to no one.<sup>16</sup>

A few operators have tried to do more. In England, Gridserve’s forecourt at Braintree set a café, a shop and a lounge beside its chargers in 2020,<sup>17</sup> and in 2025 Tesla opened a diner in Hollywood with eighty charging stalls in its car park.<sup>18</sup> Both show what a longer stop can support. Both are also commercial ventures first, and neither was designed around the community it sits in.
notes: Carroll L. V. Meeks, The Railroad Station: An Architectural History (New Haven: Yale University Press, 1956).

John A. Jakle and Keith A. Sculle, The Gas Station in America (Baltimore: Johns Hopkins University Press, 1994); Daniel I. Vieyra, “Fill ’er Up”: An Architectural History of America’s Gas Stations (New York: Macmillan, 1979).
Federal Highway Administration, “National Electric Vehicle Infrastructure Standards and Requirements,” 23 C.F.R. pt. 680 (2023).

Nana Duah, Steven Jiang, Om Prakash Yadav, Hieu Trung Nguyen, and Nastasha Earle-Young, “Navigating the Truck Parking Challenge: A Comprehensive Review of Strategies, Emerging Technologies, and Future Directions,” Transportation Research Interdisciplinary Perspectives 34 (2025): 101740, 2.
Anne-Marie Anderson and Richard J. Kish, “The Costs and Benefits of Electric Trucks: A Synopsis of the U.S. Trucking Market,” Sustainability 17 (2025): 2097.
Marc Augé, Non-Places: Introduction to an Anthropology of Supermodernity, trans. John Howe (London: Verso, 1995).
Gridserve, “GRIDSERVE Opens UK’s First Electric Forecourt,” press release, 2020.
Tesla, “Tesla Diner,” 2025, https://www.tesla.com/tesla-diner.

body: A fast charge usually takes between twenty minutes and an hour, depending on the vehicle and the charger. This study takes forty-five minutes to an hour as a typical roadside charge. For freight, the length of the stop is set by law as well as by technology. European rules stop a truck driver for forty-five minutes after every four and a half hours at the wheel,<sup>19</sup> and American rules require half an hour off after eight.<sup>20</sup> An electric truck can charge during a break the driver is already required to take. The thesis looks at all road transport, not only cars. Trucks, buses, motorcycles, bicycles and e-bikes all need somewhere to stop and charge, and each brings different people to the site.

The idea that a pause in travel produces architecture is an old one. Writing in 1894, Charles Horton Cooley noticed that settlements tend to appear wherever movement is interrupted: at a river crossing, a harbour, the end of a line, any point where a load has to be handled again.<sup>21</sup> The coaching inn, the motel, the railway station, the airport and the motorway service area can all be read this way, as buildings made from a break, each holding what its break allows. Kevin Lynch went further and treated time as something a designer works with, as real as space.<sup>22</sup> Together they give the thesis its starting principle: the time a vehicle takes to charge shapes what a site can offer the people who use it. Nikolaus Pevsner, and later Johann Friedrich Geist in his study of the arcade, followed single building types across centuries to show how each was remade by its circumstances.<sup>23</sup> This thesis treats the Powerhouse as a type that is still taking shape.
notes: Regulation (EC) No 561/2006 of the European Parliament and of the Council on the harmonisation of certain social legislation relating to road transport, Official Journal of the European Union L 102 (2006).
Maximum Driving Time for Property-Carrying Vehicles, 49 C.F.R. § 395.3.
Charles Horton Cooley, “The Theory of Transportation,” Publications of the American Economic Association 9, no. 3 (1894).
Kevin Lynch, What Time Is This Place? (Cambridge, MA: MIT Press, 1972).
Nikolaus Pevsner, A History of Building Types (Princeton: Princeton University Press, 1976); Johann Friedrich Geist, Arcades: The History of a Building Type (Cambridge, MA: MIT Press, 1983).

body: Time alone does not make a place. The history of public space shows that space offered without a reason to be there usually fails. For more than sixty years New York has let developers build bigger in return for a plaza or an arcade at street level. When Jerold Kayden’s team visited 503 of these spaces, they rated about two in every five as marginal.<sup>24</sup> William Whyte, who spent years filming people in plazas like these, found that people stayed where there was something to do and somewhere to sit, and walked past everywhere else.<sup>25</sup> Recent research has begun to measure what such places give back. A 2025 study that monitored young adults’ brain activity and stress found that third places, the cafés and gathering spaces between home and work, had restorative effects comparable to green space, working mainly through social contact.<sup>26</sup>

That is why the public space of the Powerhouse is site-specific. Its programme is set by the people who use it and by what the surrounding area lacks. In a dense city it might be a gym, a workspace or childcare. On a heavy freight corridor it might be a hostel with showers, beds and a kitchen for drivers on their rest break. In a small town it might be a market, a clinic or a community hall. In every case part of the site stays open to anyone, and whatever surrounds that open ground is chosen for the people who live, work and travel nearby. The type can adapt because its public space belongs to its site.

For the same reason, the Powerhouse is not only for people who charge. The charger anchors the site, but the open ground and the programme around it belong to anyone nearby, whether they come by car or on foot. This matters well beyond charging. Few kinds of land in America are as plentiful, or as idle, as the parking lot, which stores cars that spend most of their lives standing still.<sup>27</sup> Seen this way, the Powerhouse is a first step towards a wider claim: that any parking lot or piece of dead space could be turned towards a programme that serves its area.
notes: Jerold S. Kayden, the New York City Department of City Planning and the Municipal Art Society of New York, Privately Owned Public Space: The New York City Experience (New York: John Wiley and Sons, 2000).
William H. Whyte, The Social Life of Small Urban Spaces (Washington, DC: Conservation Foundation, 1980).
Leiqing Xu et al., “Neurological Benefits of Third Places for Young Adults in Healthy Urban Environments,” Frontiers of Architectural Research 14 (2025): 1350–1363.
Donald Shoup, The High Cost of Free Parking (Chicago: Planners Press, 2005).

body: An anchor gives a place its reason to exist. The shopping mall made the idea explicit. When Victor Gruen designed Southdale outside Minneapolis in 1956, he hoped to give a new suburb the centre it lacked.<sup>28</sup> Two department stores at either end pulled shoppers through, and the rent from the smaller shops between them paid for the covered court where people met.<sup>29</sup> The anchor created the opportunity, and everything else grew around it.

At the Powerhouse the charger plays that part. Charging creates a fixed and predictable stretch of time, and with it an opportunity: a steady flow of people with an hour to spare, arriving at the same place every day. The anchor is what turns that opportunity into a place. Programme suited to the site, whether a gym, a hostel or a market, draws on that flow to keep itself going, and its rent can pay for energy generated on site, keep charging free and look after the open ground. The mall’s anchor was a department store and its public space was private property. The Powerhouse is anchored by a piece of public infrastructure, and the place it supports is built for the community.
notes: M. Jeffrey Hardwick, Mall Maker: Victor Gruen, Architect of an American Dream (Philadelphia: University of Pennsylvania Press, 2004).
Victor Gruen and Larry Smith, Shopping Towns USA: The Planning of Shopping Centers (New York: Reinhold, 1960).

body: This thesis argues that an Electric Vehicle Powerhouse complex will turn charging activities into an opportunity for enhanced civic / community engagements. As electrification turns a five-minute stop into an hour-long charge, a charging cluster can give that hour back to people as community space, shaped by its site and supported by the programme around it.

Three questions test the argument, and each becomes a chapter. The first is about charge time: how long a roadside charge lasts for cars, freight and smaller vehicles, and whether it will stay long enough to matter as charging gets faster. The second is about public space: how much of an existing roadside site is given to community use, measured as a share of site area and leaving out parking and charging bays. The third is about the programme: what each neighbourhood lacks, and whether a programme built around the charge gives people a reason to stay. Together they form the hypothesis: the longer charging holds people on site, the more the site can give its neighbourhood, through a programme suited to the area and public space open to all. If longer charge times lead only to more retail, the hypothesis fails.

The research uses charging as the first and clearest case, and treats parking lots and other dead space as the wider field its findings are meant to reach. It compares fuel stations, highway service plazas and fast-charging sites in urban, suburban and freight-corridor settings, mainly in the United States, with precedents from the United Kingdom and Europe. To isolate the effect of charge time, it compares sites of similar size and traffic, and sets aside chargers placed at existing malls and supermarkets, where shopping draws the charger rather than the other way round. The study assumes that charging will keep taking long enough to matter. New megawatt chargers that promise hundreds of kilometres of range in five minutes challenge that assumption,<sup>30</sup> but freight rest rules, limited grid capacity at highway sites and a mixed fleet of vehicles make it likely that the hour will last for some time yet. Few site plans are public and operators guard their finances, so the funding model will be argued from precedent rather than proven.
notes: BYD, “BYD Unveils Super e-Platform with Megawatt Flash Charging for Electric Vehicles,” press release, March 2025.

body: The thesis reads the Powerhouse through three lenses, each concerned with one part of its argument: sustainability with the Powerhouse and its charging, phenomenology with the stop, and social theory with the community and its public space.

The first lens is sustainability. Sustainable development is usually defined as meeting the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own.<sup>31</sup> Here it has three parts. Environmentally, the Powerhouse builds on ground that parking already covers and makes and stores its own energy. Socially, it serves people who cannot charge at home and stays open to those who do not charge at all. Economically, its programme keeps the place running. Ian McHarg’s practice of reading a site in layers, and Sim Van der Ryn and Stuart Cowan’s principle that design should grow from its place and make natural systems visible, guide where a Powerhouse goes and how its energy is shown.<sup>32</sup>

The second lens is phenomenology: what it is like to spend the stop on site. Martin Heidegger argued that to build is to make dwelling possible, and that a built thing, like a bridge, gathers a place around it.<sup>33</sup> The charger can do the same. Christian Norberg-Schulz added that people need to know where they are and to feel that they belong,<sup>34</sup> which today’s identical charging stops rarely allow. In these terms, the Powerhouse turns a pause in a journey into a place.

The third lens is social theory. Henri Lefebvre showed that space is produced: planned by those who design it and lived by those who use it.<sup>35</sup> Charging sites today are almost entirely planned, by standards and operators, for the vehicle. Lefebvre’s right to the city, the claim that everyone may use and shape urban space,<sup>36</sup> underlies the Powerhouse’s promise of public space open to all. Michel Foucault’s account of surveillance raises the opposite risk, that such places watch and move on the people who linger.<sup>37</sup> The Powerhouse answers with Jane Jacobs’s alternative: safety that comes from people being present, not from being watched.<sup>38</sup>
notes: World Commission on Environment and Development, Our Common Future (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1987), 43.
Ian L. McHarg, Design with Nature (Garden City, NY: Natural History Press, 1969); Sim Van der Ryn and Stuart Cowan, Ecological Design (Washington, DC: Island Press, 1996).
Martin Heidegger, “Building Dwelling Thinking,” in Poetry, Language, Thought, trans. Albert Hofstadter (New York: Harper & Row, 1971).
Christian Norberg-Schulz, Genius Loci: Towards a Phenomenology of Architecture (New York: Rizzoli, 1980).
Henri Lefebvre, The Production of Space, trans. Donald Nicholson-Smith (Oxford: Blackwell, 1991).
Henri Lefebvre, “The Right to the City,” in Writings on Cities, ed. and trans. Eleonore Kofman and Elizabeth Lebas (Oxford: Blackwell, 1996).
Michel Foucault, Discipline and Punish: The Birth of the Prison, trans. Alan Sheridan (New York: Pantheon, 1977).
Jane Jacobs, The Death and Life of Great American Cities (New York: Random House, 1961).

body: The thesis is built in four layers: a question, a hypothesis, three lenses, and a sequence of chapters that tests the hypothesis and leads to a design.

The question is what a charging site could become if it were designed for the people who stop there rather than only for their vehicles. The hypothesis answers it: an Electric Vehicle Powerhouse complex will turn charging activities into an opportunity for enhanced civic / community engagements. It has three parts, and each becomes a chapter. The community stop is the time people spend on site, set by the vehicle, the charger and the law. The public space is the share of the site anyone can use without buying anything. The programme is what the neighbourhood lacks, built around the charge.
The three lenses set out in section VII run through every part: sustainability for the ground and the energy, phenomenology for the experience of the stop, and social theory for who the space is for.

The method is comparative. Rather than build a site and wait to see what happens, the thesis studies existing ones: gas stations, highway service areas, truck stops and charging hubs, in corridor, city and town settings. At each it records three things: how long people stay, how much of the site is open to them, and whether a programme serves them while they wait. The evidence comes from published specifications, site plans and aerial photographs, timed observation on site, short conversations with the people there, and first-person notes on what the stop is like.

The chapters follow this structure. Chapter 2, The Stop, defines and measures the time on site, through sustainability and phenomenology. Chapter 3, The Public Space, asks what makes people stay and what each neighbourhood needs, through phenomenology and social theory. Chapter 4, The Programme, asks how a programme can serve people and keep a place running without taking it over, through social theory and sustainability. Together they test the hypothesis.

What the chapters find becomes a set of design criteria. In Graduate Thesis 01 and 02 these are applied to a chosen site, where the Powerhouse is designed as a working building: chargers, energy, programme and public space arranged for one neighbourhood. The written thesis makes the case; the design shows what it looks like.

The hypothesis of this thesis is that an Electric Vehicle Powerhouse complex will turn charging activities into an opportunity for enhanced civic / community engagements. This chapter is about charging: understanding how it works, and in particular the length of the stop it creates. Charging comes first because it is the cause. It is the reason for the Powerhouse. The chapter defines the stop, explains how it will be measured, sets out what could make that measurement wrong, and proposes how the study will deal with each problem. It moves from the ground charging occupies, to the network it belongs to, to the history of stops that became places, and then to the three things that set the length of a stop today: the vehicle, the law and the speed of the charger. Of the three lenses set out in Chapter 1, it works mainly through two: sustainability, which looks at the ground charging occupies and the energy it needs, and phenomenology, which looks at the stop as time that is lived, not just measured.<sup>1</sup>
notes: For the three lenses, see Chapter 1, section VII.

body: American cities have covered a large share of their land in concrete, and most of it is for parking. Donald Shoup showed that free parking is paid for by everyone, in higher rents, higher prices and land that could have been used for something else, and that a parked car spends most of its life standing still.<sup>2</sup> The paid space at the curb, the private parking lot, the gas station with its forecourt, the supermarket car park and the highway rest area are all versions of the same ground: paved space sized to the vehicle and not to the person in it. It is used for a few minutes at a time and left empty for the rest.

That ground is about to change. Every mode of road transport is moving to electricity, from bicycles and scooters to cars, buses and trucks, and every one of those vehicles will need to charge. A gas station does not need anywhere to sit, because nobody is there long enough to use it. A charging site does, because the people using it have to stay for longer. The Powerhouse does not replace the concrete. It is an addition to it, a layer that turns paved ground that already exists into a third place: somewhere people spend time between home and work because the charge gives them a reason to be there.

What matters, then, is not charging in general. It is the length of the stop that charging causes. In this thesis it is defined as the time in minutes between a person arriving at a site and leaving it, on a visit whose main purpose is to charge a vehicle or to take a required rest. I call this the stop. If the hypothesis holds, the longer the stop, the more a site can give the neighbourhood around it: a programme that gives people a reason to stay, and public space open to everyone. Parking is the starting condition. It is the ground the stop already sits on, and the ground the Powerhouse proposes to give back. Reusing it, rather than paving new land, is the first sense in which the Powerhouse is sustainable: a solution that grows from the place it is in.<sup>3</sup>
notes: Donald Shoup, The High Cost of Free Parking (Chicago: Planners Press, 2005).
Sim Van der Ryn and Stuart Cowan, Ecological Design (Washington, DC: Island Press, 1996).

body: Charging is not one place but a network, and each part of it produces a different kind of stop. It helps to read it as an anatomy, from the slowest charger to the fastest.

Home and workplace. Most charging happens where the vehicle is already parked for hours. A car plugged into a wall socket or a home charger fills slowly overnight, and an office car park does the same during the working day. By the Department of Energy’s estimate, about four in five charges happen at home.4 These charges create no stop at all, because the vehicle was going to be standing there anyway.
Destination charging. Slower public chargers at supermarkets, hotels, car parks and on the street let people top up while they do something else. The stop is set by the errand, not by the charge.

Fast charging. Along highways and in city hubs, fast chargers fill a car in well under an hour. This is where the stop is created by the charge itself. The driver is there because the car needs energy, and has to wait for it. It is the closest thing to the gas station, and the clearest case for the Powerhouse.

Freight and fleet charging. Trucks, buses and delivery vans charge at depots overnight or at high-power chargers along freight routes. Freight already has a stop it cannot avoid: drivers are required by law to rest, and the places to do so are short. The lack of truck parking is one of the most pressing problems in American trucking, and drivers near the end of their legal hours keep driving to look for a space.5

Battery swapping. For scooters, and for some cars and trucks, the empty battery can be taken out and replaced with a full one. The vehicle stops for minutes, but the battery it leaves behind still has to be charged somewhere.

This anatomy creates the first problem for measuring the stop. Because most charging happens at home, the people at public chargers are a particular group: travellers on long trips, people who live in apartments or park on the street, ride-hail drivers and fleets. They are not a cross-section of all drivers, and a study of them alone could give a false picture. This is a problem of selection bias. The study responds by choosing sites that serve different users, such as a highway site used by travellers and trucks, a city hub used by residents and ride-hail drivers, and a small-town site used by local people, and by asking each visitor why they are there. It also counts people who arrive without a vehicle, since the Powerhouse is meant to be open to everyone.
notes: US Department of Energy, “National EV Charging Network,” https://www.energy.gov/topics/national-ev-charging-network.

Nana Duah, Steven Jiang, Om Prakash Yadav, Hieu Trung Nguyen, and Nastasha Earle-Young, “Navigating the Truck Parking Challenge: A Comprehensive Review of Strategies, Emerging Technologies, and Future Directions,” Transportation Research Interdisciplinary Perspectives 34 (2025): 101740, 2.

body: The link between the stop and the making of a place is old, and Chapter 1 traced it from Charles Horton Cooley’s observation of 1894 that “population and wealth tend to collect wherever there is a break in transportation.”<sup>6</sup> What matters here is how differently each type treated the person. The railway station and the airport were built around the wait, filling it with halls, shops and restaurants.<sup>7</sup> The gas station went the other way, and it barely changed for a century.<sup>8</sup> It was built for the vehicle, and the person was expected to leave as soon as possible.

The Powerhouse proposes a new type in this line: a station for electric road transport. Like the railway station, it is organised around a break in the journey. Unlike the gas station, it is designed for the person as well as the vehicle. It also has a second purpose. By making charging somewhere people want to be, it makes the switch to electric vehicles easier to choose. In phenomenological terms, it turns a pause in a journey into a place: somewhere to dwell for the length of the stop, rather than a queue to get through.<sup>9</sup>

This history suggests the method. The study does not control the length of the stop; nobody can make a car charge more slowly to see what happens. It is comparative instead. It selects existing sites where the stop is short, medium, long and overnight, and compares how much of each site is given to people. This follows the building-type studies of Pevsner and Geist introduced in Chapter 1: follow one type through many examples and look for what changes with the conditions.<sup>10</sup> The stop is therefore measured rather than manipulated, and the sites are chosen to cover its full range.

The history also warns of the most serious problem. The hypothesis says a longer stop leads to more public space, but the reverse can also be true. People stay longer at stations and service areas that give them somewhere to sit and something to eat, and truck drivers choose rest areas with better amenities and safety features.<sup>11</sup> If the study only observed that sites with more public space have longer stops, it could not tell which caused which. This is a threat to internal validity. The response is to take the length of the stop from the charger, the vehicle and the law, which are fixed before anyone decides what to build around them, and to use the time people actually stay as a check.
notes: Charles Horton Cooley, “The Theory of Transportation,” Publications of the American Economic Association 9, no. 3 (1894): 91.
Carroll L. V. Meeks, The Railroad Station: An Architectural History (New Haven: Yale University Press, 1956).
John A. Jakle and Keith A. Sculle, The Gas Station in America (Baltimore: Johns Hopkins University Press, 1994).

Martin Heidegger, “Building Dwelling Thinking,” in Poetry, Language, Thought, trans. Albert Hofstadter (New York: Harper & Row, 1971); Yi-Fu Tuan, Space and Place: The Perspective of Experience (Minneapolis: University of Minnesota Press, 1977), 6.
Nikolaus Pevsner, A History of Building Types (Princeton: Princeton University Press, 1976); Johann Friedrich Geist, Arcades: The History of a Building Type (Cambridge, MA: MIT Press, 1983).
Duah et al., “Navigating the Truck Parking Challenge,” 9.

body: The length of the stop depends first on what arrives. Charging time is set by two numbers: how much energy the battery holds, measured in kilowatt-hours (kWh), and how fast the charger can deliver it, measured in kilowatts (kW). Dividing the first by the second gives a rough time. A 75 kWh car battery charged from 10 to 80 percent needs about 52 kWh. At 100 kW that takes about half an hour; at 50 kW, about an hour; on a 7 kW home charger, most of a working day.<sup>12</sup> Small vehicles need little energy and can charge from a wall socket. Trucks sit at the far end. Anderson and Kish note that charging an electric truck can take up to eight hours, while refuelling a diesel truck takes “a mere five to ten minutes.”<sup>13</sup> Table 2.1 sets out the range.

The table groups the stop into four lengths. A short stop is under fifteen minutes. A medium stop is fifteen minutes to an hour, which is a car at a fast charger. A long stop is one to three hours, typical of buses, large vehicles and trucks at fast chargers. An overnight stop is eight hours or more. These lengths match the lengths of stay used in Chapter 4 to choose a programme for the site.

Charge time, however, is not the same as waiting time. A car may need forty minutes of charge, but the driver may leave after twenty because they have enough to get home, or stay long after it finishes because they are eating. Some drivers never leave the car and spend the stop on their phones. If the study measured only the charge, it would describe the machine, not the person. This is a problem of construct validity.

The response is simple. The study records both: the time the vehicle needs to charge, worked out from Table 2.1, and the time people actually stay, observed on site using the timed counts developed by William Whyte and by Jan Gehl and Birgitte Svarre.<sup>14</sup> The difference between the two is the point. A charging site that only holds people for as long as the charge takes is still a forecourt. The Powerhouse aims for people to stay longer than they have to, because the place is worth staying in. Observation is kept consistent by visiting each site at the same times of day, over several days, and nobody is identified.
notes: Author’s calculation: 70 percent of a 75 kWh battery is 52.5 kWh; 52.5 kWh at 100 kW is about 32 minutes, at 50 kW about 63 minutes, and at 7 kW about 7.5 hours.
Anne-Marie Anderson and Richard J. Kish, “The Costs and Benefits of Electric Trucks: A Synopsis of the U.S. Trucking Market,” Sustainability 17, no. 5 (2025): 2097, 5.
William H. Whyte, The Social Life of Small Urban Spaces (Washington, DC: Conservation Foundation, 1980); Jan Gehl and Birgitte Svarre, How to Study Public Life (Washington, DC: Island Press, 2013).

body: For professional drivers, the length of the stop is set partly by law rather than technology. In the United States a truck driver may drive no more than eleven hours after ten consecutive hours off duty, and must take a thirty-minute break after eight hours of driving.<sup>15</sup> In the European Union a driver of a truck or coach must take a break of at least forty-five minutes after four and a half hours at the wheel, and a daily rest of at least eleven hours, which may be shortened to nine.<sup>16</sup> Table 2.2 places these rules in the same four lengths as the vehicles.

These rules apply however fast the truck charges. A required rest that coincides with a required charge is a long stop that is very likely to happen, which makes freight the most stable case for this study and the first one it tests.

Charger standards set the stop for cars. The federal National Electric Vehicle Infrastructure standards require funded highway stations to offer at least four fast-charging ports, each able to deliver 150 kilowatts at the same time.<sup>17</sup> That figure is a practical baseline for highway stops over the next decade, because it is what public money is building, and it is the figure used to calculate the charge time at highway sites.

Zoning decides what may be built around the charger. Local codes were largely written for gas stations and parking lots, and they shape whether a charging site can include food, seating, workspace or rooms to stay. The Powerhouse does not fit those categories. It is not a plaza added to a car park; it works like a third place with charging at its centre, which is a different way of using the ground altogether. Its programme comes from the needs of the area around it. On a highway or freight corridor it might be somewhere to stay, with rooms and showers for drivers on their required rest. In a city it might be a gym or a place to work. In a town without one, it might be a medical centre.

This affects how much of the site is given to people more than the length of the stop itself, and it is taken up in Chapters 3 and 4. For this chapter, zoning matters because two sites with the same stop may give very different amounts of ground to people simply because one is allowed to and the other is not. The study records the zoning of each site so that its effect is not mistaken for the effect of the stop.
notes: Maximum Driving Time for Property-Carrying Vehicles, 49 C.F.R. § 395.3.

Regulation (EC) No 561/2006 of the European Parliament and of the Council on the harmonisation of certain social legislation relating to road transport, Official Journal of the European Union L 102 (2006), arts. 7–8.
Federal Highway Administration, “National Electric Vehicle Infrastructure Standards and Requirements,” 23 C.F.R. pt. 680 (2023).

body: The stop is a moving target. Charging is getting faster. In 2025 BYD announced a one-megawatt “flash charging” system that it claims adds around 400 kilometres of range in five minutes.<sup>18</sup> Battery swapping points the same way, replacing a whole battery in minutes. If these spread, the car stop could fall back towards the length of a fuel stop within the life of the buildings this thesis proposes. Cooley saw something similar with the railways: as transfers improved, small breaks disappeared. In his words, “the number of breaks represents the expense of transportation.”<sup>19</sup>

That does not undo the thesis. A faster stop for the driver does not mean less charging overall. The energy still has to come from somewhere, and a battery swapped out of a vehicle in five minutes still needs hours to recharge. Flash charging at a megawatt draws on the grid far harder than a slow charger, and needs storage and supply close by. The Powerhouse can be that place: the swap centre where batteries are held and recharged, and the local source of power, generating and storing its own electricity for the vehicles around it. It is meant to be a powerhouse in the literal sense, solving transport’s need for electricity as well as the person’s need for somewhere to be. This is the sustainability lens at its most literal: the site produces energy as well as using it.<sup>20</sup>

This also changes what the stop depends on. If the charge no longer forces people to stay, they will stay only where the site gives them a reason, which is the role of the programme, and why the hypothesis does not rest on charging time alone. The study allows for this in three ways. It puts most weight on the stops that technology does not control, such as the required rest for drivers, which will still apply when a truck can charge in minutes. It uses the four lengths of stop rather than exact minutes, so a site only has to stay within the same range. And it asks which parts of the programme would still work if the stop were halved. Because the Powerhouse is a charging hub, energy store and third place at once, it can adapt as vehicles and charging change, rather than becoming obsolete with them.
Summary

The stop is where this thesis begins: the time a person spends at a site whose main purpose is to charge a vehicle or take a required rest. It sits on ground that parking already occupies, within a network where most charging happens at home, and it continues a long history in which the break in a journey became a place. Its length is set by the vehicle, the law and the speed of the charger, and it ranges from a few minutes to most of a day. The study compares existing sites across four lengths of stop, recording both the time the charge needs and the time people actually stay.

The main challenges are that public-charger users are not typical drivers, that a good site can lengthen the stop as well as respond to it, that charge time is not the same as time on site, that zoning can shape a site as much as the stop does, and that faster charging may shorten the stop. The responses are to study different kinds of sites and users, to take the stop from the charger, vehicle and law and use observation as a check, to record the person as well as the plug, to note each site’s zoning, and to rest the argument on required breaks and ranges of stop rather than on charger speed. Even as charging gets faster, the Powerhouse remains a source of power for transport and a place worth stopping in. Read through sustainability, the stop sits on reused ground and draws on energy made on site; read through phenomenology, it is time that can be lived rather than waited out. Chapter 3 turns to that place, through phenomenology and social theory.
notes: BYD, “BYD Unveils Super e-Platform with Megawatt Flash Charging for Electric Vehicles,” press release, March 2025.
